title: Team reflection and acting safely without evidence
blurb: Lead or join a useful team debrief, reflect in a way that changes practice, and make safe, shared, documented decisions when the evidence is weak or missing.
question: A woman asks her midwife whether a practice she has read about will help her labour. There is no good quality evidence either way and no guideline covers it. What is the safest approach?

teach.body: SPM 5.9 asks midwives to contribute to team reflection to improve practice and services; SPM 5.13.1 includes individual and team reflection, problem solving and planning; SPM 5.7 asks midwives to act safely where there is an absence of good quality evidence. In plain English: look back together to learn, and when the research does not give an answer, do not guess alone. Reason it through with the woman and the team, then write it down.

teach.caption: Any structured model works; the point is moving from description to a change in practice.

teach.body: After an emergency or a difficult birth, a short team debrief soon afterwards, and a fuller review later, help the team learn and look after each other. Keep it supportive and focused on the system: what helped, what got in the way, what we will change. Include everyone who took part, whatever their role. Learning from what went well matters as much as from what went wrong (SPM 5.3).

teach.h: When the evidence is weak or absent
teach.body: Code 6.1 asks for evidence-based advice; NICE guidance is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account alongside each woman's needs and preferences. Where good evidence is missing, use the best available evidence, be honest with the woman about what is and is not known, ask experienced colleagues (Code 13.3), agree an individual plan with her, set review points, and document your reasoning. Montgomery requires you to share material risks and reasonable alternatives.
teach.cite: NMC Code 6.1, 13.3; NICE 'Your responsibility'; Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11

teach.body: Yasmin, a healthy woman at 39 weeks, asks midwife Kemi whether a herbal remedy will help her labour start. Kemi finds no NICE recommendation and no good quality studies. She tells Yasmin honestly that the evidence is lacking and safety in pregnancy is not established, talks with the senior midwife and pharmacist, and agrees with Yasmin that she will not take it while they discuss her other options. Kemi records the conversation and plan.

teach.caption: Revalidation reflective accounts link to the Code and must not identify anyone.

teach.text: 'No evidence' is not the same as 'evidence of no effect'. It also does not mean 'do whatever you prefer'. You still give honest information, seek advice, agree a plan and document why.

items: Team reflection should be supportive, include everyone involved and end in a change to practice.
Learn from what went well as well as what went wrong.
NICE guidance is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account with each woman's needs.
Without good evidence: be honest, share material risks and options, seek senior advice, agree and record a plan.
Reflections move from description to analysis to action and never identify a woman or baby.

summary: You can now take part in team reflection that leads to change and use a structured model to reflect on your own practice. You can also make safe, shared and documented decisions when good quality evidence is missing.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a team reflection after a difficult birth, according to SPM 5.9?
options: To improve practice and services
To decide which person made the error
To prepare statements for a complaint
To complete the incident form
A.why: SPM 5.9: contribute to team reflection activities to promote improvements in practice and service.

whyNot.1: Reflection focuses on system learning, not blaming individuals.
whyNot.2: Complaint statements are a separate process.
whyNot.3: Incident reporting is separate; reflection is about learning.

A.q: A woman asks about a practice for which there is no good quality evidence and no guidance. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Tell her it is safe as no harm is reported
Advise against it as it is unproven
Explain the uncertainty and agree a plan
Let her decide without advice
A.why: SPM 5.7: act safely where good evidence is absent. Be honest about uncertainty, share risks and alternatives, seek advice and agree a documented plan with her.

whyNot.0: Absence of reported harm is not evidence of safety.
whyNot.1: A blanket refusal ignores her preferences and the shared decision.
whyNot.3: She decides, but with honest information and professional input, not left alone.

A.q: What is the status of NICE guidance for a midwife's practice?
options: It is a legal requirement in every case
It overrides the woman's preferences
It applies to doctors more than midwives
It must be taken fully into account
A.why: NICE guidance is not mandatory; professionals take it fully into account alongside the individual's needs, preferences and values.

whyNot.0: NICE guidance is not mandatory law.
whyNot.1: It is applied alongside the woman's needs and preferences, not over them.
whyNot.2: It applies to all health professionals using it.

B.q: After a shoulder dystocia, the coordinator arranges a debrief. Which approach is most likely to improve care?
options: A supportive whole-team discussion soon after
A meeting for the midwife and doctor involved
A written statement from each person
A discussion at next month's audit meeting
B.why: A supportive debrief with everyone involved, soon after the event, captures what helped and hindered while it is fresh and supports staff.

whyNot.1: Leaving out others misses their view and support needs.
whyNot.2: Statements are for investigation, not shared learning and support.
whyNot.3: A month later loses detail and the chance to support staff early.

B.q: A woman at term declines continuous CTG that her guideline recommends and asks for intermittent auscultation. What should the midwife do?
options: Apply the CTG as the guideline requires
Discuss risks, agree a plan and document it
Transfer her care to the obstetric team
Ask her partner to persuade her
B.why: SPM 1.20–1.22: respect her right to decline, advocate for her when her decision is outside guidance, minimise risk and keep the relationship; document the discussion and plan.

whyNot.0: Monitoring without consent breaches her right to decline.
whyNot.2: Obstetric input may help, but she still needs midwifery care and a shared plan.
whyNot.3: Pressure through her partner undermines her autonomy.

B.q: A midwife is writing a reflective account about a postnatal haemorrhage for her revalidation. Which detail must she leave out?
options: How she felt during the emergency
What she would do differently
The woman's name and date of birth
The part of the Code it relates to
B.why: Revalidation records must not contain information that could identify a woman or baby.

whyNot.1: Learning and future action are the point of reflection.
whyNot.3: Each reflective account must link to the Code.

C.q: A midwife caring for a woman with a rare condition finds no guideline and limited evidence on intrapartum care. What should she do first?
options: Follow the plan used for a similar condition
Search for a case report and follow it
Ask the woman what she would like to happen
Seek advice from the senior midwife and MDT
C.why: Code 13.3: ask for help when something is beyond your competence. Without guidance, an experienced MDT agrees a plan with the woman, which is documented and reviewed.

whyNot.0: A plan for a different condition may not be safe here.
whyNot.1: A single case report is weak evidence to follow alone.
whyNot.2: Her wishes matter, but she needs expert information to decide.

C.q: Team reflections over three months keep raising delays in getting theatre staff for urgent caesareans. What should happen next?
options: Record the theme and continue debriefing
Ask staff to raise it individually
Wait for an incident to prove the point
Turn the theme into an improvement project
C.why: SPM 5.9 and 5.13.1: team reflection should lead to problem solving, planning and improvement, such as a QI project with the theatre team.

whyNot.0: Recording without action does not improve care.
whyNot.1: A shared theme needs a team response, not separate complaints.

C.q: A midwife reads one small study suggesting a new pushing technique shortens the second stage. It is not in NICE or local guidance. What is the best approach?
options: Use it with her next women in labour
Discuss the evidence with the team first
Tell women it is proven to work
Dismiss it as it is not in guidance
C.why: One small study is weak evidence. Discussing it with the team lets it be appraised and, if promising, introduced through governance rather than by one person.

whyNot.0: Changing practice on one small study, without agreement, is unsafe.
whyNot.2: One small study does not prove effect.
whyNot.3: Research should be appraised and discussed, not dismissed.

reteach.title: Honest, shared, written down
reteach.question: What three things make a decision safe when the evidence runs out?

blocks.body: Honest: tell the woman what is known and not known, including material risks and reasonable alternatives. Shared: bring in senior and multidisciplinary colleagues and decide with her, not for her. Written down: record the information given, the plan and your reasoning, with review points.

blocks.text: 'No evidence of harm' does not mean 'safe'.

explain.body: Midwives must be able to act safely in situations where there is an absence of good quality evidence: drawing on the best available evidence, experience, colleagues and the woman's own values.

test.q: When there are no randomised trials on a question, what should a midwife's practice be based on?
options: Personal preference
The most recent news report
What was done in training
The best available evidence
test.why: Where high-level evidence is missing, practice draws on the best available evidence, experience and consensus, with honest discussion and review.

whyNot.0: Preference is not a sound basis for care.
whyNot.1: News reports are not research evidence.

explain.body: For revalidation, a midwife discusses her five reflective accounts with another NMC registrant in a reflective discussion.

test.q: Who must a midwife hold her revalidation reflective discussion with?
options: Another NMC registrant
Her line manager, whatever their profession
A university lecturer
A service user representative
test.why: The reflective discussion must be with another NMC registrant.

whyNot.1: A line manager can confirm, but the discussion must be with an NMC registrant.
whyNot.2: A lecturer would need to be an NMC registrant.
whyNot.3: Service user feedback is a separate requirement.

explain.body: Montgomery: take reasonable care to ensure the woman knows of any material risks of recommended treatment and of reasonable alternatives. Uncertainty itself can be material.

test.q: Under Montgomery, what must a midwife make sure a woman knows about before she consents?
options: Every possible complication
The risks the midwife thinks are important
Material risks and reasonable alternatives
The cost of each option to the NHS
test.why: Montgomery para 87: material risks of recommended treatment and reasonable alternatives.

whyNot.0: The test is materiality, not every conceivable risk.
whyNot.1: Materiality is judged from the woman's position, not the professional's.
whyNot.3: Cost is not part of the Montgomery duty.

explain.body: A-EQUIP's restorative function supports midwives after difficult events and its formative function uses guided reflection to develop knowledge and skills.

test.q: A midwife is shaken after a stillbirth on her shift. Which A-EQUIP function is designed to support her wellbeing?
options: Normative function
Formative function
Restorative function
Personal action for quality improvement
test.why: The restorative function (clinical supervision) supports wellbeing and has been shown to reduce stress and burnout.

whyNot.0: Normative concerns monitoring, evaluation and quality control.
whyNot.3: Personal action for QI concerns improving care quality.
